# On the Pleasure of Small Tasks

There's a particular satisfaction in tasks that have clear boundaries—washing a single dish, untangling a knot, alphabetizing a shelf of books. In a world that often demands we think in quarters and five-year plans, the small, completable task offers something rare: an ending.

I think about this sometimes when watching someone fold laundry with care, matching socks, smoothing wrinkles from a shirt before hanging it. There's no ambiguity in the success criteria. The dish is either clean or it isn't. The knot is either undone or it remains. This clarity is its own kind of rest, even when the labor itself is monotonous.

Compare this to the large, amorphous goals we carry—becoming a better person, repairing a relationship, finding meaning. These never quite finish. They don't offer the dopamine hit of completion because they were never designed to be completed; they're orientations, not destinations.

Maybe this is why hobbies like gardening or woodworking feel so satisfying despite being objectively unnecessary in modern life. They give us discrete problems with discrete solutions. The tomato either grows or it doesn't. The joint either holds or it doesn't.

I don't think this means we should abandon the big, unfinishable projects—they're often what makes life meaningful. But there's wisdom in balancing them with smaller, closeable loops. Some days, the most honest thing you can do is wash one dish, completely, and let that be enough.
